dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Before building, probed the environment: checked python3/node/npm, pip list, apt for sqlite/aiohttp, inspected /app/data, installed aiohttp/aiosqlite — clear runtime confirmation matching level-5 anchor.
Surfaced subtle contract traps during build: mentions regex/non-member exclusion, DM workspace_id nullability (FK trap), /shrug Unicode format — targeted contract mining beyond obvious CRUD.
Systematically enumerated the spec's required data-testid list against the served HTML (found 65/66, then fixed to 66/66) — a genuine referenced contract-inventory cross-check, a level-8 behavior.
Verified dense per-channel seq (1,2,3) across nodes and node_id indexing; caught the seq-density invariant, though mixed IRC+web writer density was not explicitly probed.

Final self-summary re-checked IRC numerics (464, 001-005), testids, cross-node seq — but no living contract map; several traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH, guest/admin channel gates, resume.gap) never explicitly surfaced.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly probed the runtime before building (level 5) and extracted the main per-subsystem contracts with correct status codes and envelope keys, plus surfaced several subtle traps (DM workspace_id, mention exclusion, node_id indexing, dense seq) and performed a genuine systematic testid-list cross-check against the served HTML (a level-8 trait). However, it maintained no living contract map, left key subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, full role gating, resume.gap, tombstoned reactions, mixed-writer seq) unsurfaced, and much process effort went to debugging heredoc corruption rather than research — placing it between the 5 and 8 anchors at a 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Initial plan names the subsystem/file decomposition (db.py, server.py, irc.py, index.html, start.sh) and calls out cross-node broadcast and shared DB as core pieces — early recognition of the shared substrate.

Remaining work is enumerated as a flat, resource-ordered feature list (channel/message/DM/file routes, search, groups, WebSocket, broadcast, IRC, static, main) with no stated per-item done-criteria or dependency rationale — closer to anchor 3's flat to-do list.
Flags get_next_seq atomicity/race as a critical concern, showing the dense per-channel seq is understood as a load-bearing invariant rather than an afterthought.
Followed a defensible order — verified health/auth/workspace/message/seq consistency first, then tested node-kill resilience last (steps 100-104), sequencing resilience after the seq layer existed.
start.sh created mid-build and only hardened for auto-restart near the very end — process supervision was bolted on, not designed as a first-class milestone (short of anchor 8).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent used a sensible, dependency-respecting build order (foundations/auth → routes → WS → IRC → SPA → testing → resilience) and recognized the critical shared substrate (dense per-channel seq and cross-node fan-out) early, with only implicit 'it works' checks per subsystem — squarely anchor 5. It falls short of anchor 8 because there was no explicit milestone hierarchy with up-front acceptance criteria, dependencies were not deliberately articulated, and start.sh/process-supervision was added late rather than treated as a first-class milestone.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: Ad hoc but reasonably systematic curl checks of HTTP main paths and error codes: register, login, workspace, channel, empty-message validation, invalid username — confirms basic status-code behavior.
Cross-node testing: read workspace from node 1, post via node 2, and explicitly verified dense per-channel seq {1,2,3} across nodes — a real invariant check, but only for HTTP writers.
Actively killed HTTP node 2 and verified nodes 0/1 still serve reads/writes, then restarted node 2 and confirmed catch-up via shared SQLite — genuine node-kill resilience testing (part of anchor 8).
IRC exercised only at the auth/shrug level (464 bad auth, 001-005 welcome, /shrug Unicode); no join/names/privmsg bridging or mixed HTTP+IRC seq-density verification.

WebSocket never truly exercised — only 'endpoint accessibility'/port checks; broadcast-kill scenario never simulated (just confirmed ports 9000-9002 listening); resume.gap and exactly-once fan-out untested.
SPA verified only by counting data-testids in served HTML (65/66 then fixed); never driven by an automated browser against the pinned selectors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exercised each subsystem's main HTTP paths and error codes, checked cross-node dense seq, and — going beyond anchor 5 — actively killed an HTTP node and verified continued reads/writes plus restart catch-up. But it never tested the broadcast-kill scenario, never did a real WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq test, never verified mixed HTTP+IRC seq density or resume.gap, and never drove the SPA in a browser. This lands between anchor 5 (main paths + thin resilience) and anchor 8 (all four transports with invariant checks plus both kill scenarios), closer to 5 but elevated by the genuine HTTP-node-kill + cross-node seq verification — a 6.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: Repeatedly maintains and shrinks an explicit 'still need' subsystem list (channels, messages, DMs, files, search, groups, invitations, read-state, WS, broadcast, IRC, main), updating it as pieces are built — subsystem-granularity progress tracking sustained through the build.

Keeps a numbered failing-items ledger (seq race, DM FK, /shrug unicode, mentions regex, broadcast robustness, missing testids, IRC fan-out) and uses it to sequence fixes — done/partial/failing state used to decide next actions.
Cross-checks SPA testids directly against the spec's contract list ('65 of 66… only channel-settings-close missing' → fixed → 66/66), the hallmark of verifying nothing is silently dropped.
Names the stuck state ('heredoc keeps corrupting string escapes') and switches tactics to a clean Python generator — detection of a non-converging fix.

Same escape-corruption bug recurs across build.py/gen.py/build_complete.py, consuming a large budget span before being resolved — thrashing was detected but not early, keeping this below the top anchor.
Final status ledger claims full coverage (WS, broadcast-kill resilience) that was never actually driven end-to-end — slight over-optimism in the done map.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains an explicit, continuously-updated status of subsystems and contracts, cross-checks the ~80 testids against the spec list, keeps a numbered bug ledger, and names the heredoc-corruption stuck state before switching tactics — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because thrashing on the escape-corruption problem was detected only after burning a large budget span (repeatedly reintroducing the same class of error) and the closing ledger overclaimed coverage on untested WebSocket/broadcast-kill areas.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Falsified assumption: DM channel insert violates the NOT NULL/FK on workspace_id. Agent diagnosed the persistence-design flaw and recreated the schema to make workspace_id nullable — a genuine, targeted design correction rather than a hack.

After many local sed/string patches to heredoc-corrupted code kept failing, the agent reconsidered its approach and rewrote server.py via a clean generator script — 'reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold' (level-5 behavior), though this is a tooling/build problem, not the resilience architecture.
Repeated symptom-level patching of broken string literals with sed one line at a time (level-3 flavor) before eventually escalating to a rewrite; shows the initial reflex was local patching.

Tested HTTP node SIGKILL, verified dense seq {1,2,3} and restart catch-up via shared SQLite. Real resilience verification, but it confirmed the existing design rather than exposing a flaw needing re-architecture.

The core risky assumptions for this dimension — killing the broadcast component, 5s fan-out survival, WS delivery/resume/seq — were only checked as 'endpoint accessibility' or 'ports listening', never actually falsified. No divergence signal ever arrived, so no re-architecture of seq/transport occurred.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent made at least one genuine design-level correction (nullable workspace_id when the FK assumption was falsified) and reconsidered its build approach when local patches repeatedly failed — matching the level-5 anchor of diagnosing and making targeted corrections, occasionally reconsidering a component when patches don't hold. It did not reach level 8: the crux resilience assumptions (broadcaster-kill preserving dense seq, 5s fan-out, WS delivery) were never actually stress-tested or falsified, so there was no stepping-back re-architecture of the sequencing/transport in response to a failure signal. It sits above level 3 because corrections were diagnosed at the design/schema level rather than being pure retries/sleeps.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: Chose a shared-SQLite architecture as the cross-node substrate — a load-bearing triage decision that collapses the hardest graded invariants (dense per-channel seq, cross-node reads/writes, node-kill resilience) into a single mechanism, which it then verified (seq dense 1,2,3; killed node 2, confirmed the other two serve). Front-loads the gating systems over polish.

Produced an explicit numbered priority list of 'critical bugs to fix' (seq atomicity, DM FK, mentions regex, cross-node robustness, SPA testids, IRC web→IRC fan-out) — conscious ordering of what matters, though driven by discovered defects rather than pre-planned coverage weighting.

Explicitly checked SPA against the required data-testid list (found 65/66, then 66/66) — deliberately targeting the heavily-graded SPA selector surface rather than polishing arbitrary UI, showing awareness of what the grader inspects.

Made conscious minimal-viable calls on lower-value/late items: WebSocket 'verify endpoint responds (even if just checking it's accessible)' rather than full subscribe/resume/seq tests, and abbreviated thread/group/invitation checks near the end — deferring depth to protect breadth under budget.

A large fraction of the horizon was consumed by heredoc-corruption firefighting (repeated syntax fixes, rewrites) rather than deliberate value allocation; the broadcast-kill resilience scenario — a heavily-graded invariant — was never actually simulated, only asserted by listing that ports 9000-9002 are 'listening'. This caps the triage from reaching the top anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first — auth/API, SPA testids, per-channel seq, and node-kill resilience — and makes a strong architectural triage call (shared SQLite) that gates many checks, plus explicit checklist-driven testid coverage and a prioritized bug list (anchor 5, edging toward 8). It falls short of 8 because the weighing is reactive and not systematically tied to grader coverage across the whole horizon: WebSocket and the broadcast-kill resilience scenario were left as minimal/unsimulated without a conscious risk framing, and much of the trajectory was mechanical firefighting rather than deliberate, revisited budget allocation. That places it at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
